Git & GitHub: A
Hands-On Lab
Version control you'll actually use —from
your first commit to your first pull request
Why Developers Live in Git
No more zip folders
One project, a history of committed versions.
Safe to experiment
Try changes on a branch before merging them.
Teamwork without chaos
Combine changes and resolve conflicts together.
A portfolio that is public
Public repositories can showcase your work.
Theory First: What Is Version Control?
Version control system (VCS)
Records committed versions so you can revisit saved states and inspect who changed what, and why.
1. Copy the folder
project_final_v3.zip
Manual copies lack built-in history,
authorship and merge tools.
2. Centralized (SVN, CVS)
A central server manages the
shared history.
Offline: keep editing files. Server-
dependent commits and history
queries must wait.
3. Distributed (Git)
A normal full clone includes project
history.
Commit and branch offline. Shallow
or partial clones may omit history or
objects.
Git supports local commits, lightweight branches and distributed collaboration.
What Git Actually Stores
Delta-based storage
Some systems reconstruct file versions from a base plus
stored differences.
Git: snapshots
A commit references a snapshot of the tracked files staged
for that commit.
blob
The contents of one file.
tree
A folder listing: names pointing at
blobs and other trees.
commit
A tree, zero or more parents,
author/committer metadata and a
message.
9f4a1c7e2b8d3a05f6c1e94b7d20a3c8ef15b6d2
Changing an object changes its ID. Rewriting history creates new commits with new IDs.
The Commit Graph
a1b2c3 d4e5f6 7a8b9c e1f2a3
main
Commits reference their parents. A root has none, and a merge can have more than one.
A branch is a pointer
A name pointing at a commit.
Creating a branch is lightweight.
HEAD is where you are
Usually points to your current
branch. In detached HEAD mode, it
points to a commit.
Two merge outcomes
A fast-forward moves a pointer. A
typical merge of diverged branches
has two parents.
Merging can require conflict resolution. Review the result before sharing it.
How Git Thinks
Working Directory
The files you are editing right
now.
Staging Area
The file versions selected for
your next commit.
Repository
Stored snapshots and
metadata, usually in .git
git add git
commit
A commit records the staged snapshot, its metadata and a message explaining the change.
Lab 0: Set Up Git
~ bash / zsh (Linux, macOS or WSL)
git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@college.edu"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list
Do this once
Once per OS user account. Project
settings can override these defaults.
Match your GitHub email
Use an email linked to GitHub, or your
GitHub no-reply address.
Before starting: install Git 2.28+ and a text editor. These settings identify commits, not a GitHub login.
Lab 1: Your First Repo
1 Create 2 Track 3 Commit 4 Review
mkdir hello-git && cd hello-git
git init
printf "# Hello Git\n" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git log --oneline
Check: the log shows Add README. Next, edit README.md, save, stage and commit again.
Lab 2: Look, Then Undo
See what changed
git status
git diff
git log --oneline --graph
git diff shows unstaged edits. Use git diff --staged to
inspect staged changes.
Choose one undo action
git restore README.md
Discard unstaged edits (restore from index).
git restore --staged README.md
Unstage while keeping your file edits.
git revert HEAD
Reverse the latest commit with a new commit.
Warning: restore discards unstaged edits. Revert may conflict. Run one action only after checking status.
Lab 3: Branch and Merge
main
feature/readme
git switch -c feature/readme
printf "\nBranch practice\n" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Update README"
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/readme -m "Merge README"
A merge commit here
--no-ff creates a two-parent
merge commit. Without it, this
lab fast-forwards.
GitHub = Git + Teamwork
Git manages local history. GitHub hosts repositories and collaboration tools.
Backup
Keep a remote copy of the commits
you push.
Pull requests
Propose a change, get it reviewed,
then merge.
Issues
Track bugs and tasks where the
code lives.
Actions
Configure a workflow to run tests on
pushes.
Pages
Publish a static project website.
Student Pack
Education benefits for verified
students.
Lab 4: Push to GitHub
First, on github.com
1 New repository
2 Name it hello-git
3 No README, license or .gitignore
~ replace YOU with your GitHub username
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/hello-git.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
Later on main: git push. A new branch needs its own first push.
HTTPS: use a credential manager or personal access token, not your account password. SSH needs an SSH
remote URL.
Lab 5: How Teams Really Work
1 Set up access
Your partner invites you to hello-git in
Settings > Collaborators. Accept the
invitation.
2 Start outside your own repo
Replace OWNER with their username.
Run the commands on the right.
3 Review on GitHub
Open a pull request: base main, compare
docs-update. Partner reviews and
merges.
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/hello-git.git pair-lab
cd pair-lab
git switch -c docs-update
printf "\nReviewed with a partner\n" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Update README"
git push -u origin docs-update
Check: a reviewed, merged pull request. Then run git switch main and git pull --ff-only origin main.
Habits of a Clean Repo
Do this
Commit small and often – one idea per commit
Write messages like: Fix login redirect
Use git pull --ff-only. If it refuses, ask for help.
Add a README so people can run your code
Never do this
Never commit keys, passwords or .env files
No vague messages like: fixed stuff
Do not force-push a shared branch
Do not commit node_modules or build output
Never push secrets, even to private repos. If exposed, revoke or rotate them immediately.

C Example: First Working Version
Linux, macOS or WSL: Git 2.28+, a POSIX shell, C compiler and standard-library headers. Complete Lab 0.
1 Create the project folder
mkdir c-git-lab
cd c-git-lab
2 Save this as main.c in that folder
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
printf("Sum = %d\n", 2 + 3);
return 0;
}
3 Run it, then record version 1
gcc -Wall -Wextra main.c -o demo && \
./demo
printf "demo\ndemo.exe\n" > .gitignore
git init -b main
git add main.c .gitignore
git commit -m "Add sum program"
Ignore rules cover demo and demo.exe only.
Check: the program prints Sum = 5. Git now has your first commit.
C Example: A Change on a Branch
Continue in the same c-git-lab folder. Change one line so the difference is easy to see.
4 Create a branch and edit main.c
git switch -c feature/new-sum
Replace the printf line with:
printf("Sum = %d\n", 10 + 20);
Save the file. Keep the include line, main function
and return statement unchanged.
5 Test, inspect and commit the edit
gcc -Wall -Wextra main.c -o demo && \
./demo
git diff
git add main.c
git commit -m "Change sum to 30"
6 Compare with the original version
git diff main..feature/new-sum
Check: output is Sum = 30. The diff shows 2 + 3 replaced by 10 + 20.
C Example: Review and Merge on GitHub
Use your own GitHub account. Set up HTTPS authentication before pushing, as in Lab 4.
7 Create empty c-git-lab on GitHub (no README, license or .gitignore)
8 Replace YOU with your username, then publish both branches
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/c-git-lab.git
git push -u origin main
git push -u origin feature/new-sum
9 Open and merge a pull request
On GitHub: base = main, compare = feature/new-sum.
Review Files changed, then merge the pull request.
10 Bring the merged version to your laptop
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
Final check: gcc -Wall -Wextra main.c -o demo && ./demo | Expected: Sum = 30
